reference.source: Bradley and Daroff Neurology in Clinical Practice
clinicalPearls: Autosomal dominant disorder most often caused by haploinsufficiency of NKX2-1 (TITF1), a transcription factor essential for development of the brain, lung and thyroid
Chorea typically begins in infancy or early childhood and is characteristically non-progressive or even improves with age, distinguishing it from Huntington disease
The wider brain-lung-thyroid syndrome links the movement disorder with congenital hypothyroidism and neonatal or childhood respiratory disease
Motor milestones may be delayed and gait can be affected, but cognition is usually relatively preserved
Other movement features such as myoclonus, dystonia and motor tics may coexist with the chorea
A positive family history with an early-onset, comparatively stable chorea should prompt consideration of NKX2-1 testing
Recognition allows screening and treatment of associated thyroid and pulmonary problems and appropriate genetic counselling
reference.pathophysiology: Benign hereditary chorea is usually caused by heterozygous loss-of-function variants or deletions involving NKX2-1 on chromosome 14, a homeobox transcription factor that guides development of striatal interneurons, thyroid follicular cells and lung parenchyma. Haploinsufficiency disturbs the migration and differentiation of basal-ganglia interneurons, producing chorea without the relentless striatal degeneration seen in Huntington disease, which explains the relatively benign, non-progressive course. Because the same gene directs thyroid and lung morphogenesis, deficiency also produces congenital hypothyroidism and respiratory disease, unifying the brain-lung-thyroid phenotype.
additionalDifferentials: Huntington disease and Huntington disease-like disorders
Sydenham chorea and other post-infectious/autoimmune chorea
Cerebral palsy with a dyskinetic component
additionalInvestigations: NKX2-1 molecular genetic testing including deletion analysis
Thyroid function tests to detect congenital or acquired hypothyroidism
Chest imaging and respiratory assessment for associated lung disease
Brain MRI, which is typically normal or non-specific
Copper studies and caeruloplasmin to exclude Wilson disease
Antistreptococcal and autoimmune screen where post-infectious chorea is possible
redFlags: Clearly progressive chorea or cognitive decline, which argues against a benign course and for an alternative diagnosis
reference.prognosis: The chorea of NKX2-1-related disease is generally non-progressive and often lessens through adolescence and adulthood, with a broadly favourable neurological outlook. Overall prognosis is mainly determined by the associated thyroid and pulmonary features, which respond to appropriate treatment.
pitfalls: Labelling early-onset chorea as cerebral palsy and missing a treatable, inheritable syndrome
Overlooking associated hypothyroidism or lung disease because attention is fixed on the movement disorder
Assuming any childhood chorea is Sydenham chorea without considering a genetic cause
Expecting relentless progression and prompting unnecessary alarm when the natural history is benign
